## Code sharing in Ecology

![](images/2026_07_16_code-sharing/cooper-2026-cover.png){fig-alt="Cover of Cooper et al. 2026, Methods in Ecology and Evolution, with the title 'Data- and code-archiving in the British Ecological Society journals: Present status and recommendations for future improvements'."}

1861 ecology papers from 7 journals (2017-2024)

## Sharing code is still the exception (?)

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- Data is always shared, code not
- Shared code is often not sufficient
    - missing a README (39%)
    - low-quality READMEs
    - missing license (26%) or wrong license
    - ...

:::

::: {.column}


![[Cooper et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.70338), *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*](images/2026_07_16_code-sharing/cooper-2026-figure.png){fig-alt="Bar chart from Cooper et al. 2026: nearly all papers that used data archived it, but only about a third of papers that used code archived the code."}

:::

:::



## Why?

- Time pressure - not a priority
- Journals still often don't require it
- Code is not part of peer review
- Not sure how to do it properly

## Code sharing is worth it

- Open science creates trust
- Reproducibility: Results can be verified
- Reusability: Others (including future you) can build on your work
- Visibility: Credit, collaborations
- A portfolio of your coding skills

## Today

- How to build and publish a good practice repository: the most important things to do
- Focus on data analysis projects
- Where AI tools can help

. . .

At the end you will have:

- Checklist to prepare your own repo for publication
- Some AI prompts to use for building and auditing your project

## What we will not talk about

- Research software (packages, libraries, tools)
- Writing code (Good coding practices, style, functions, testing, etc ...)
    - For this check out the lecture [R code that lasts](https://selinazitrone.github.io/tools_and_tips/sessions/10_r-code-that-lasts.html) and some other resources linked on the website
- Too many language specific details (but some R and Python hints)

# Structure & orientation {.inverse}
> Can someone understand it?

## Use a conventional folder structure

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

- Separate your files into folders
- Most important: separate data, code, and output
- Separate raw data (read-only) from processed data (produced by scripts)
- Follow a template or use your own structure, as long as it is clear and consistent
    - [rrtools](https://github.com/benmarwick/rrtools) (R), [Cookiecutter Data Science](https://cookiecutter-data-science.drivendata.org/) (Python)

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```
temperature-resistance/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── growth_assay.csv
│   └── clean/
│       └── cleaned_data.csv
├── analysis/
│   ├── 01_clean-data.R
│   ├── 02_fit-models.R
│   └── 03_make-figures.R
└── output/
    ├── figures/
    │   └── linear-model-fit.png
    └── tables/
        └── model-results.csv
```
Our messy project, sorted into folders

## Use informative file names

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

- Human readable: reveal the content
- Machine readable: no spaces, no special characters
- Work with default ordering: left-padded numbers or YYYY-MM-DD dates first

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.fragment}

::: {.nonincremental}

```
temperature-resistance/
├── data/

│       └── cleaned_data.csv
├── analysis/

│   └── 03_make-figures.R
└── output/
    ├── figures/
    │   └── linear-model-fit.png
    └── tables/
        └── model-results.csv
```

## Add a thorough README

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- README's are the entry point to your project
- A README should be a simple text format (plain text or Markdown)

:::

::: {.column}

```
temperature-resistance/
├── README.md
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── growth_assay.csv
│   └── clean/
│       └── cleaned_data.csv
├── analysis/
│   ├── 01_clean-data.R
│   ├── 02_fit-models.R
│   └── 03_make-figures.R
└── output/
    ├── figures/
    │   └── linear-model-fit.png
    └── tables/
        └── model-results.csv
```

:::

:::

## What a README should do

At minimum, a README should answer:

::: {.nonincremental}

- **What** the project is, and which **paper** it belongs to
- **How to run it** (how to install, which order to run the scripts)
- **How the files are structured** (what is in each folder, what the files are)
- **How to cite** the project
- **Who to ask** when it breaks

:::

## A README skeleton

```markdown
# Temperature and antibiotic resistance in soil bacteria

Code and data for: Baldauf et al. (2026), *Journal*, doi:10.xxxx/xxxxx

Cite as: Baldauf et al. (2026). Data and code for "Temperature and antibiotic resistance in soil bacteria". doi:10.xxxx/xxxxx

Code is licensed under MIT, data under CC-BY-4.0. See `LICENSE` and `data/LICENSE` for details.

## How to run

Download or clone the repository to run it locally.

The project needs R version 4.0.0 or higher.

1. Restore the environment: `renv::restore()` - This will create a project library and install all required packages.
2. Run `main.R`, which runs all analysis scripts in order

## Project structure

- `analysis/`      analysis scripts, run in numerical order
- `data/raw/` the original growth-assay measurements (read-only)
- `data/clean/` cleaned data produced by the scripts
- `output/` figures and tables produced by the scripts

### `analysis/`

- `01_clean-data.R`: cleans the raw data and saves it
    - Input: `data/raw/growth_assay.csv`
    - Output: `data/clean/cleaned_data.csv`
- `02_fit-models.R`: fits the models and saves the results table
    - Input: `data/clean/cleaned_data.csv`
    - Output: `output/tables/model-results.csv`
- `03_make-figures.R`: makes the manuscript figures
    - Input: `data/clean/cleaned_data.csv`, `output/tables/model-results.csv`
    - Output: `output/figures/linear-model-fit.png` (Figure 2)

### `data/`

See `data/README.md` for a codebook of all variables.

## Contact
selina.baldauf@fu-berlin.de
```

> Can someone rerun it?

## Make the run order obvious

. . .

**Level 1**: Number your scripts `01_`, `02_`, etc. and add this to the "How to run" section in the README.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

```md
## How to run

1. Install dependencies with `renv::restore()`
2. Run the scripts in numerical order:
    1. `01_clean-data.R`
    2. `02_fit-models.R`
    3. `03_make-figures.R`

```

:::

::: {.column}

```
temperature-resistance/
├── README.md
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── growth_assay.csv
│   └── clean/
│       └── cleaned_data.csv
├── analysis/
│   ├── 01_clean-data.R
│   ├── 02_fit-models.R
│   └── 03_make-figures.R
└── output/
    ├── figures/
    │   └── linear-model-fit.png
    └── tables/
        └── model-results.csv
```

:::

:::


## Make the run order obvious

**Level 2**: Create a **main script** that calls all scripts in order, so this is the only file someone needs to open.


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### main.R

```r
# Run the whole analysis pipeline

# Step 1: Clean the data
# Input: `data/raw/growth_assay.csv`
# Output: `data/clean/cleaned_data.csv`
source("analysis/01_clean-data.R")
# Step 2: Fit the models and produce table 1
# Input: `data/clean/cleaned_data.csv`
# Output: `output/tables/model-results.csv`
source("analysis/02_fit-models.R")
# Step 3: Make all manuscript figures
# Input: `data/clean/cleaned_data.csv`, `output/tables/model-results.csv`
# Output: `output/figures/linear-model-fit.png` (Figure 2)
source("analysis/03_make-figures.R")
```

### main.py

```python
# Run the whole analysis pipeline
from clean_data import main as clean_data
from fit_models import main as fit_models
from make_figures import main as make_figures

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Step 1: Clean the data
    # Input: `data/raw/growth_assay.csv`
    # Output: `data/clean/cleaned_data.csv`
    clean_data()
    # Step 2: Fit the models and produce table 1
    # Input: `data/clean/cleaned_data.csv`
    # Output: `output/tables/model-results.csv`
    fit_models()
    # Step 3: Make all manuscript figures
    # Input: `data/clean/cleaned_data.csv`, `output/tables/model-results.csv`
    # Output: `output/figures/linear-model-fit.png` (Figure 2)
    make_figures()
```

:::

:::

::: {.column}

```
temperature-resistance/
├── README.md          
├── main.R
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── growth_assay.csv
│   └── clean/
│       └── cleaned_data.csv
├── analysis/
│   ├── 01_clean-data.R
│   ├── 02_fit-models.R
│   └── 03_make-figures.R
└── output/
    ├── figures/
    │   └── linear-model-fit.png
    └── tables/
        └── model-results.csv
```


:::

:::

## Make the run order obvious

**Level 3**: Use **workflow management tools** like [targets](https://books.ropensci.org/targets/) (R) or [Snakemake](https://snakemake.readthedocs.io/en/stable/)
(any language). Define workflows, automatically run the steps in the right order and only rerun what changed.

![An example workflow from the [targets package](https://books.ropensci.org/targets/walkthrough.html)](images/2026_07_16_code-sharing/targets-workflow.png){fig-alt="A workflow diagram from the targets package, showing how the scripts depend on each other and which outputs they produce."}

## Record all dependencies and versions

Let people know what they need to install to make the code work.

:::{.nonincremental}

- The language itself and its version (e.g. R 4.4.1, Python 3.12)
- All libraries/packages and their versions
- Any other programs your code calls

:::

## Record all dependencies and versions

**Level 1**: Copy-paste dependencies into the README. Easy, but less convenient for people who need to install the software.

. . .

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

::: {.nonincremental}

- Run `sessionInfo()` at the **end** of your pipeline (so every package is loaded), then paste the package list into the README.
- `renv::dependencies()` also lists the packages your code uses, but without versions.

:::

```r
sessionInfo()
#> R version 4.4.1 (2024-06-14)
#> ...
#> other attached packages:
#> [1] ggplot2_3.5.1 dplyr_1.1.4   readr_2.1.5
```

### Python

::: {.nonincremental}

- Run `pip freeze` **inside** your project's **virtual environment**, then paste the list into the README.
- `pipreqs` (install with `pip install pipreqs`) scans your code for the packages you actually import, like `renv::dependencies()`.

:::

```bash
$ pip freeze
pandas==2.2.2
numpy==1.26.4
matplotlib==3.9.0
```

:::

## Record all dependencies and versions

**Level 2**: Snapshot your local environment so users can recreate them easily.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

::: {.nonincremental}

Use the [`renv` package](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/) to:

- `renv::init()`: set up a project library and record all packages in a `renv.lock` file
- `renv::snapshot()`: update your lockfile with new packages
- `renv::restore()`: recreate the environment on another machine

:::

### Python

::: {.nonincremental}

Use [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) to:

- `uv init`: set up a project that records dependencies in a `pyproject.toml`
- `uv add pandas`: install a package and pin all exact versions in a `uv.lock` file
- `uv sync`: recreate the environment on another machine (including the right Python version)

:::

:::

## Record all dependencies and versions

**Level 3**: Package the whole environment in a **container** (e.g. [Docker](https://www.docker.com/)) so the code runs identically on any machine. Powerful but also more to learn and maintain.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

::: {.nonincremental}

- The [Rocker project](https://rocker-project.org/) gives you different R images to build on.

:::

### Python

::: {.nonincremental}

- Start from an official [`python` base image](https://hub.docker.com/_/python) (e.g. `python:3.12-slim`) and install your dependencies in it
- [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/integration/docker/) also provides Docker images
- **No Dockerfile needed:** [repo2docker](https://repo2docker.readthedocs.io/) builds the image from a `requirements.txt` or `environment.yml`

:::

:::

## Use paths relative to project root

- Paths anchored to the project root work on any machine, from any working directory
- Absolute paths (`C:/Users/selina/PhD/...`) will break the project

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

Use an R project (`.Rproj`, in RStudio or Positron) and the [`here` package](https://here.r-lib.org/). `here()` finds the root by searching upward for a marker (`.Rproj`, `.git`, `.here`), independent of the working directory:

```r
library(here)
read.csv(here("data", "raw", "growth_assay.csv"))
```

### Python

Use the [`pyprojroot` package](https://pypi.org/project/pyprojroot/), the equivalent of R's `here`. It also has a `here()` function that finds the root, so paths resolve correctly from everywhere:

```py
from pyprojroot.here import here
import pandas as pd
pd.read_csv(here("data/raw/growth_assay.csv"))
```

:::

## Set a seed for anything random

- Many random processes like sampling, bootstrapping, simulations, even plots with jittering
- Don't forget to set a random seed so that the results are reproducible

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```r
set.seed(42)
```

### Python

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
```

:::

# Data {.inverse}
> Can someone understand the data situation?

## Save your data in open formats


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- Save data in **open formats**: `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.parquet`, etc.
- Avoid proprietary formats: `.xlsx`, `.sav`, `.dta`, etc.

:::

::: {.column}

```
temperature-resistance/
├── README.md          
├── main.R
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── growth_assay.csv
│   └── clean/
│       └── cleaned_data.csv
├── analysis/
│   ├── 01_clean-data.R
│   ├── 02_fit-models.R
│   └── 03_make-figures.R
└── output/
    ├── figures/
    │   └── linear-model-fit.png
    └── tables/
        └── model-results.csv
```

:::

:::


## Document your data files

Describe all your data files: Variable names, units, missing data codes, and other relevant information.

E.g. one table per file:

::: {.fragment}

| Variable | Meaning | Unit / coding |
|----------|---------|---------------|
| `sample_id` | Unique sample identifier | text |
| `temp` | Incubation temperature | °C |
| `resistant` | Grew on antibiotic plate | 0 = no, 1 = yes |
| `mic` | Minimum inhibitory concentration | mg/L |

:::

## Document your data files

- Add documentation to the main README
- Or create a separate `data/README.md` for all data files

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

Main README:

```md

### `data/`

The `data/` folder contains the raw and cleaned growth assay measurements. See `data/README.md` for all variables.

```

:::

::: {.column}

```
temperature-resistance/
├── README.md          
├── main.R
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── growth_assay.csv
│   └── clean/
│       └── cleaned_data.csv
├── analysis/
│   ├── 01_clean-data.R
│   ├── 02_fit-models.R
│   └── 03_make-figures.R
└── output/
    ├── figures/
    │   └── linear-model-fit.png
    └── tables/
        └── model-results.csv
```

:::

:::

## What if you cannot share the data?

- **Data too big**: Use a separate data repository (Zenodo, Dryad, Figshare, etc.) and link to it in the README. If you can: include a download script in your code to get the data.
- **Restricted data**: Include a statement about where and how to request access in the README. Add a codebook in `data/README.md` so the code can be reviewed even without data
- **Closed data**: Include synthetic example data along with the code that generated it, so the pipeline runs end to end. Include a statement in the README that the real data cannot be shared. 

# Licence & citation {.inverse}
> Can someone legally reuse and cite it?

## Add a licence

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- Without a licence file, people can not reuse your code
- Most popular licences in ecology are:
    - Creative commons licences (CC0, CC-BY)
    - MIT & GNU General Public License (GPL)
- Careful: CC licenses are NOT for code, only data & text


:::

::: {.column}

![Number of licences used for code and data in BES ecology papers. [Cooper et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.70338), *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*](images/2026_07_16_code-sharing/cooper-2026-license-no-cc.png){fig-alt="Bar chart from Cooper et al. 2026: the licences used in archived code and data, showing that CC is very common."}

:::

:::

## Which licence to choose?

- Are there specific requirements for your project?
- Checkout [choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com) to guide through licence choice

. . .

Standard open licences:

| Licence | What it does | For |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| [CC0](https://choosealicense.com/licenses/cc0-1.0/) | Public-domain waiver, no attribution required | Data |
| [CC BY](https://choosealicense.com/licenses/cc-by-4.0/) | Reuse for any purpose, attribution required | Data |
| [MIT](https://choosealicense.com/licenses/mit/) | Permissive: reuse freely, keep the notice | Code |
| [GNU GPL v3](https://choosealicense.com/licenses/gpl-3.0/) | Copyleft: derivatives stay open, same licence | Code |

:::{.aside}

Further reading: The [Turing way book](https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/licensing/) on licensing; [A case for CC0](https://blog.datadryad.org/2023/05/30/good-data-practices-removing-barriers-to-data-reuse-with-cc0-licensing/) by theDRYAD repository

:::

## How to add a licence

Many different ways. In general: Add a `LICENSE` file containing the licence text
into the repository.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```r
# writes a LICENSE file for you
usethis::use_mit_license("Your Name")
# or:
usethis::use_gpl3_license()
```

### GitHub

Add file → Create new file → name it `LICENSE` → **"Choose a license template"**

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```
temperature-resistance/
├── README.md
├── LICENSE
├── main.R
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── LICENSE
│   ├── raw/
│   └── clean/
├── analysis/
└── output/
```

:::

:::

## Make your code citable

**Level 1**: a "How to cite" section in the README (always good to have).

```markdown
## Citation
Baldauf et al. (2026). Code and data for "Temperature and antibiotic resistance in
soil bacteria". https://doi.org/10.xxxx/xxxxx
```

## Make your code citable

**Level 2**: add a `CITATION.cff` file

::: {.nonincremental}

-   A small YAML file that you can create with [`cffinit` website](https://citation-file-format.github.io/cff-initializer-javascript/) and add to your project
-   GitHub then shows a **"Cite this repository"** button with ready-made APA / BibTeX
-   Zenodo reads it when it archives your release, so the credit is correct automatically
-   Add your **ORCID** so the credit points at *you*, not just your name

:::

## The "Cite this repository" button

::: {.callout-note}
## IMAGE PLACEHOLDER: `github-cite-button.png`

Screenshot of a GitHub repo with the **"Cite this repository"** button open (right sidebar), showing the APA / BibTeX dropdown. Ideally the same real repo used for the README screenshot in section 1.

:::

## Ready to publish?


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

Some final checks before you publish:

- Leave any junk files? Any `_DS store`, ...
- Do a practical reproducibility check:
  - Send it to a friend
  - Test the project on another machine

:::

::: {.column}

```
temperature-resistance/
├── README.md          
├── LICENSE            
├── CITATION.cff       
├── main.R
├── DESCRIPTION
├── renv.lock
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   ├── clean/
│   └── README.md  
├── analysis/
└── output/
```

:::

# Archive & publish {.inverse}
> Can someone find the exact version you used?

## Can I just publish it on Github?

- Github is a standard place to develop and share code
- The benefit of Github: 
    - Easy to find and share
    - Nice display of README, LICENCE, etc.
- BUT: It is not an archive where a specific version of the code is frozen

## Archive your data and get a DOI

- Archiving your data means freezing a specific version of it
- Upload your project to a repository like [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org), [Dryad](https://datadryad.org/), [Figshare](https://figshare.com/), or a domain-specific repository
- You will get a DOI (Digital Object Identifier) for that version of your project

:::{.callout-tip}

You can link your GitHub repo to Zenodo to archive your project directly.

:::


## Add your DOI to the README and the paper

Once you have a DOI, add it in two places:

- the code README (Zenodo gives you a nice copy-paste badge)
- the manuscript: "Code and data are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.xxxxx (v1.0)."

## The whole thing, as a checklist

Have a look at the checklist on the website for your own repos.

There is a **one-page version** you can print and cross off, and a **longer version** with explanations and examples.

::: {style="font-size: 65%;"}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**1. Structure & orientation**

::: {.nonincremental}
-   [ ] Data, code, output in separate folders
-   [ ] File names say what files do or contain
-   [ ] README: what, how to run, who to ask
:::

**2. Running it**

::: {.nonincremental}
-   [ ] Run order obvious (numbers, README, or main script)
-   [ ] No absolute paths, no `setwd()`
-   [ ] Dependencies + versions recorded (incl. language)
-   [ ] Seeds set for anything random
:::

**3. Data**

::: {.nonincremental}
-   [ ] README states the situation (open / restricted / synthetic)
-   [ ] Codebook: variables, units, coding
-   [ ] Open formats; raw data separate and read-only
-   [ ] Last look: no unintended sensitive data, no junk
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**4. Licence & citation**

::: {.nonincremental}
-   [ ] A `LICENSE` file exists
-   [ ] Code and data licensed separately
-   [ ] Citable: README section, ideally `CITATION.cff`
:::

**5. Archive & publish**

::: {.nonincremental}
-   [ ] Release/tag marks the paper's version
-   [ ] Archived with a DOI (switch on **before** the release)
-   [ ] DOI in README and manuscript
:::

**Final test**

::: {.nonincremental}
-   [ ] A colleague ran it from scratch
:::

:::

:::

:::

# AI can help you in 2 ways {.inverse}
> 1. Create READMEs
> 2. Audit your repo against the checklist

## The ground rules


- The AI needs **access to your repo**
    - an IDE assistant (e.g. Claude Code, GitHub Copilot) - I use Claude Code in Positron
    - ChatGPT via Codex
    - a browser upload
- Use it as a helper, not an authority (revise drafts, think whether suggestions are plausible)

## AI help to draft the README

- AI is good at the tedious part: listing files, what they do, inputs/outputs, ...
- Use a good prompt that describes how the README should look like
- Let AI generate a draft that you review

## Example prompt for a README draft

Read it and adjust the parts you don't like

```text
Read every file in this repository. Draft a README.md with these sections:
- Title, a one-sentence description, and the paper it belongs to
- How to run: dependencies (with install commands) and the order to run the scripts
- Project structure: what each folder and script does, with inputs and outputs
- How to cite, and who to contact
Use only what you find in the files. If something is missing (no licence, no
citation, ...), say so instead of inventing it. Keep it concise and in Markdown.
```

## Example prompt for a data codebook

Read it and adjust the parts you don't like

```text
For every data file in `data/`, produce a codebook as a Markdown table with one
row per variable: name, meaning, unit or coding, and type. Note any missing-value
codes. Infer this from the data files and the code that creates them, but do not
guess meanings you cannot support: mark those "TODO". Output one table per file,
under a heading with the file name.
```

## AI audit of your repo against the checklist

- Finalize your repository with the help of the checklist
- Before you publish: Point the AI at your repo and ask it for an audit
- Limitations: Might come up with false positives or false negatives, so **always check the findings yourself**
- How to mitigate: Use a good prompt 

## Example prompt to audit your repo

:::{.callout-note}

Here a good prompt for an AI audit of your repo, ready to copy-paste into your AI tool.
:::

## The repo reviewer tool

- Project output from code sharing workshop
- Developed with Tessa and Rebecca
- Work in progress
- Usable as a copy-paste prompt or an AI agent skill.



Point it at your repository. It checks against criteria like today's checklist and writes a **plain-language, prioritised report**:

## You do not need our tool to start

Any AI assistant that can read files can run a lite version **today**:

```text
You are reviewing a research code repository for publication readiness.
Check it against these criteria and nothing else:
1. Orientation: README with purpose, run instructions, contact?
2. Rerunnability: clear run order? dependencies with versions? absolute paths?
3. Data: is the data situation stated? is there a codebook?
4. Legal: licence file? citation information?
5. Archive: a release or archived version with a DOI?
For each problem: name the file (or what is missing), why it matters,
and the smallest fix. Sort by priority. Do not invent files you have not seen.
```

. . .

This is the short version. The **full prompt** is on the session page, ready to copy.

# Conclusion {.inverse}

## Summary

- Shareable ≠ perfect: Start with one thing
- Follow checklist
- Use AI tools
